This is true whether the final vowel is long or short, and whether the final syllable is open CV(V) or closed CV(V)C. new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is on the final syllable regardless of vowel length or syllable shape; every word is stressed; no secondary stress. The only exceptions are systematic: words bearing the lexical H pitch accent whose final vowel is short carry the tone on the penult, and stress retracts to the penult so tone and stress coincide (tonal words with a final long vowel keep final stress). Analysed as a right-aligned iamb, switching to a trochee when tone forces penultimate accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 591: 'Barring the consideration of clitics, main word stress is final and there is no evidence of secondary stress.' p. 592: 'Stress is obligatory in Uspanteko; tone is not' (ex. 1) - all words bear stress, only some bear tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal words ending in a short vowel take penultimate tone and stress (e.g. [wálib'] 'my daughter-in-law', [áb'aj] 'stone', [íwir] 'yesterday', p. 596, data from Can Pixabaj 2006:56); tonal words with a final long vowel keep final stress with tone on the first mora. Clitic integration discussed in the Appendix. Cites Campbell 1977 and Can Pixabaj 2006 as agreeing on default final stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Uspanteko as spoken in and around the municipality of Uspantán (Tz'unun Kaab'), department of Quiché, Guatemala, from the authors' own fieldwork (2010-2021) plus Can Pixabaj 2006; no dialect split is reported. The 2023 paper notes that neighbouring Cunenteco (usually classed as a K'iche' dialect) may also have tone but it is not described.

new_statements.quote: The basic stress system of Uspanteko is straightforward. In toneless words, stress falls on the word-final syllable, essentially without exception. There are no secondary stresses. This pattern of stress assignment is exemplified by the toneless words in Fig. 2, and is the same pattern of stress assignment found in other K'ichean-branch Mayan languages, none of which have tone (DiCanio & Bennett 2021, Bennett 2016, England & Baird 2017). [...] In words of this type, tone is realized on the penultimate syllable, and stress retracts to the position of tone (Figs. 4-10). [...] (We know that stress retraction is specifically driven by H tone because this is the only context in which penultimate stress is ever observed.)

new_statements.rule_in_words: In toneless words stress is word-final essentially without exception, with no secondary stresses, as in other K'ichean languages; in tonal words with only short vowels the H tone sits on the penult and stress retracts to it, which is the only context where penultimate stress occurs. Stress is cued by duration, intensity and vowel quality; tone by raised f0.

new_statements.quote: Stress in non-tonal words is final (e.g. kaminaq [ka.mi."naqʰ] 'dead'). Contrastive long vowels only occur in word-final stressed syllables (e.g. k'echelaaj [kʼe.tʃe."la:χ] 'forest'). Tone is restricted to the last two syllables of the word, and interacts with stress. Tone coincides with stress on final long vowels, as in incháaj [in."tʃá:χ] 'my ash'. In a word with a final short vowel, like wíxk'eq ["wíʃ.kʼeqʰ] 'my fingernail', lexical tone appears on the penult, and stress retracts to the same position.

new_statements.rule_in_words: In toneless words stress is final, no secondary stress; long vowels only in final stressed syllables; H tone always on the penultimate mora and stress always on the tonal syllable, so tonal words with only short vowels have penultimate stress. Analysed as a right-edge iamb (default) vs. trochee (tonal short-vowel words). Vowel syncope targets the foot-internal unstressed vowel (pretonic under final stress, posttonic under penultimate stress).
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal words with only short vowels take penultimate stress (e.g. inkínaq' [ʔin.ˈkí.naqʼ] 'my bean', ajxójil [ʔaχ.ˈʃó.χil] 'dancer', p. 403). Prefixes and suffixes can bear stress and tone (p. 425 area, ápix 'your tomato', jporiil 'its roughness').

new_statements.quote: Primary stress occurs by default on the rightmost syllable of the word in Uspanteko. There is no evidence of secondary stress. In these respects, the Uspanteko stress system resembles the stress systems of related K'ichean-branch Mayan languages, which also strongly tend towards fixed final stress [...] (p. 25 of 42). Stress can also occur on the penultimate syllable, but only in words bearing lexical high tone (p. 26 of 42). [...] In words with final short vowels, the interaction of tone and stress is more complex. When the final vowel is short, tone can only occur on the penultimate syllable. Stress then retracts to coincide with tone (p. 28 of 42).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog final stress encodes fixed final stress; the article confirms default rightmost primary stress with no secondary stress, and adds that stress is penultimate in the subclass of words carrying lexical high tone on a short-vowel penult (tone on the penultimate mora, stress retracts to coincide with it). Same default placement, plus a tone-conditioned exception class the catalog record does not encode.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default primary stress on the word-final syllable (cued by duration on short vowels; long vowels and coda [ʔC] clusters licensed only in final stressed syllables). The language also has contrastive, morphologically controlled lexical high tone restricted to the penultimate mora of the word: on a final long vowel tone and stress are both final; when the final vowel is short, the high tone sits on the penult and stress retracts to the penult to coincide with it (e.g. aqan [ʔa.ˈqan] 'leg' vs. wáqan [ˈwá.qan] 'my leg'). Penultimate stress does not license long vowels.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly none: 'There is no evidence of secondary stress.' (p. 25 of 42)
new_statements.exceptions: Penultimate stress in words with lexical/morphological high tone and a final short vowel (tone-driven stress retraction); related K'ichean languages noted to have loanword and a few lexical/morphological exceptions to final stress; penultimate tone (hence penult stress) normally blocked in words ending in [ʔC] clusters and largely in words with final long vowels.
new_statements.identity_note: The article describes Uspanteko (ISO usp) as spoken in San Miguel Uspantán, El Quiché, Guatemala; no sub-dialect restriction is stated for the stress facts, though the authors note that sources differ on the tones they report.

tone_statements.quote: this paper argues that there is one incorrect basic assumption in the approach advertised in [1], viz. that Uspanteko has lexical tone. Instead, I propose that both the tonal contrasts as well as the interactions with vowel quality derive from contrastive foot structure in the underlying representation. One consequence of the approach is that the tonal surface differences derive solely from the mapping of intonational tones, a prominence tone H* and a word-final boundary tone L; no tonal information is stored in the lexicon.

tone_statements.n_tones: No lexical tones (H* + L boundary intonational; contrast carried by foot type)

tone.says: Possessive-prefix stem allomorphy (stress/pitch accent shifts, vowel length alternations, consonant deletion) analysed with underlying metrical templates (syllabic iambs, moraic trochees); pitch accent contrasts are a surface exponent of trochaic feet (falling tone) vs iambic feet (H level tone), against the cophonology account of Bennett & Henderson 2013.

sources.quote: this paper argues that there is one incorrect basic assumption in the approach advertised in [1], viz. that Uspanteko has lexical tone. Instead, I propose that both the tonal contrasts as well as the interactions with vowel quality derive from contrastive foot structure in the underlying representation. One consequence of the approach is that the tonal surface differences derive solely from the mapping of intonational tones, a prominence tone H* and a word-final boundary tone L; no tonal information is stored in the lexicon.
